text: Getting back to @browserdotsys's question, which I know he is anxious to have answered, you will generally find that lower-grade brands of paint are actually more consistent in their drying times (and often faster drying) than higher-grade brands.

@browserdotsys This is because, basically, the highest grade brands of paint consist of oil+pigment, and the chemistry and texture falls out however it may, where student grade stuff usually contains modifiers to make it consistent between colors.

@browserdotsys Anyway, I recommend using high quality paints--if they're too expensive, paint with cheaper pigments in an expensive line rather than cheaper paints--and simply learning to use the variable drying times to your advantage.

This is related to, but not identical, to another pair of terms you'll hear: "direct vs indirect painting".  No indirect painting is alla prima, and some but not all direct painting is alla prima.
Broadly, direct painting is painting where the visible effect--that is, what the viewer actually sees--is given by an opaque surface layer of paint
Whereas indirect painting uses various forms of transparency to create a visual effect caused by the action of multiple layers of paint simultaneously.
Alternately, say you paint an entire figure monochromatically, getting the form and light, and then glaze over it with transparent paints to give the thing color.  This is indirect painting.
(There is obviously a spectrum here, it's not a firm binary)
